sources.source_title: National Consumer Helpline: E-commerce Grievance Guidance

sections.title: Online order not delivered or refund not received
sections.text: For an online order that was not delivered, arrived incorrectly, or was not refunded, preserve the order confirmation, invoice, payment record, promised delivery date, tracking status, seller details, and customer-support messages. Contact the seller or platform through its official grievance channel, clearly request delivery, replacement, or refund as appropriate, and keep the written complaint acknowledgement or reference number. Do not make another payment to unlock a refund.

sections.title: Escalating an unresolved e-commerce consumer grievance
sections.text: The Department of Consumer Affairs National Consumer Helpline accepts consumer grievances through its official web portal and helpline 1915. If the seller or platform does not resolve an e-commerce complaint, the consumer can register the grievance with the available evidence and keep the NCH docket number for follow-up. This is consumer-grievance guidance; use cybercrime.gov.in or 1930 when the facts indicate cyber financial fraud rather than an ordinary delivery, quality, cancellation, or refund dispute. Cyber Saathi must not promise a refund or legal outcome.

sources.source_title: Citizen Financial Cyber Frauds Reporting and Management System

sections.title: Urgent financial fraud reporting
sections.text: For a suspected unauthorized bank, wallet, card, or UPI transaction, act promptly. The National Cybercrime Reporting Portal guidance directs victims to call 1930 or report at cybercrime.gov.in. Preserve the transaction screenshot and keep the bank or wallet name, transaction ID, transaction date, relevant account or UPI details, and any acknowledgement available. Do not share OTP, PIN, password, or send more money.

sections.title: After calling 1930: acknowledgement number and the 24-hour portal complaint
sections.text: The Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre states that complaints about financial cyber fraud can be reported by calling the national helpline 1930, where an official records the details on the complainant's behalf. After the acknowledgement number arrives by SMS, the complainant is required to make a formal complaint on the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal within 24 hours using that acknowledgement number. Calling the helpline alone does not complete the complaint.

sources.source_title: National Cybercrime Reporting Portal Citizen Manual: Other Cyber Crime

sections.title: Phishing and account compromise evidence
sections.text: For a phishing email or suspected account compromise, preserve original evidence. Save the email as PDF or EML when possible, retain screenshots, email headers, relevant attachments, the suspicious URL, and the approximate incident date and time. Do not delete the original email, header, screenshot, or attachment before you have recorded the evidence needed for a report.

sections.title: Harassment, abuse, and cyberstalking evidence
sections.text: For cyber bullying, stalking, sexting, threatening messages, or abusive social-media content, preserve the original chat, message, profile ID, page URL, and screenshots. Platforms may offer reporting or flagging controls under their own policies. The portal manual lists Online and Social Media Related Crime categories for cyber bullying, stalking, sexting, and related reports.

sections.title: Impersonation, malicious attachments, and device risk
sections.text: A fake profile or impersonating email can be reported with the relevant profile ID, URL, screenshots, service-provider details, and approximate date and time. The portal manual also warns that malicious email attachments can install malware or capture saved credentials. Preserve evidence and avoid opening suspicious attachments or sharing one-time passwords.

sources.source_title: National Cybercrime Reporting Portal FAQ: Women and Child Reporting

sections.title: Women and child safety reporting boundary
sections.text: The National Cybercrime Reporting Portal has a Women and Child reporting section and a Report Other Cybercrimes section. Its FAQ describes anonymous reporting only for specified online sexually explicit content; it must not be presented as anonymous reporting for every incident. For any report, keep the complaint details accurate and complete. If there is immediate danger, seek local emergency help as well as preserving safe evidence.

sections.title: Evidence a complainant should keep, and how the portal protects it
sections.text: The National Cybercrime Reporting Portal FAQ lists the material a complainant may keep and upload, including a credit-card receipt, bank statement, online money-transfer receipt, a copy of an email, the URL of a webpage, chat transcripts, a screenshot of a suspect mobile number, videos, images, and any other relevant document. The portal generates a hash value for an uploaded file so the integrity of the digital evidence can be established later. Keep the original material; do not edit or redistribute it.

sections.title: Reporting anonymously, or with your name: what changes
sections.text: The National Cybercrime Reporting Portal offers two routes for a women- or child-related cybercrime, and only for that category. Report Anonymously lets you file without giving any personal information at all - the portal states this explicitly for online rape and gang-rape content - while the information about the incident itself must still be accurate and complete. Report and Track asks for your name, phone number and email address, and in return you receive an SMS and email with a complaint reference number, and you can log in and follow the progress of the complaint. That reference number and the ability to follow the case come with the Report and Track route. Neither route is the braver or the more correct one: a person who is afraid of being identified can still report, and a person who wants the case followed through can give their details. Both go to the police.

sources.source_title: राष्ट्रीय साइबर अपराध रिपोर्टिंग पोर्टल: अक्सर पूछे जाने वाले प्रश्न

sections.title: हिंदी में रिपोर्टिंग और साक्ष्य
sections.text: राष्ट्रीय साइबर अपराध रिपोर्टिंग पोर्टल पर महिलाओं और बच्चों से जुड़े अपराध तथा अन्य साइबर अपराध की रिपोर्टिंग के अलग विकल्प हैं। उपलब्ध साक्ष्य जैसे बैंक स्टेटमेंट, ऑनलाइन धन-अंतरण की रसीद, ई-मेल की प्रति, वेबपेज URL, बातचीत की प्रतिलिपि और संदिग्ध नंबर के स्क्रीनशॉट सुरक्षित रखें। किसी पहचानकर्ता की रिपोर्ट को अपराध का प्रमाण न मानें।

sources.source_title: National Cybercrime Reporting Portal: Suspect Repository and Report Suspect

sections.title: Suspicious identifier handling
sections.text: The National Cybercrime Reporting Portal describes facilities to search or report suspect mobile numbers, email IDs, account numbers, URLs, messaging handles, SMS headers, and social-media URLs. A reported or matched identifier is not proof that a person is a criminal. Cyber Saathi must not claim live access to the portal or return a live match; it can direct a citizen to the official portal and preserve the identifier for review.

sources.source_title: National Cybercrime Reporting Portal: Cyber Safety Tips

sections.title: General cyber safety
sections.text: The National Cybercrime Reporting Portal publishes cyber safety tips for protecting people, data, and devices. Treat unexpected links, attachments, and requests for passwords, PINs, or one-time passwords with caution. For a suspicious but unclear event, do not invent a diagnosis: ask what happened, preserve relevant evidence, and use the official reporting route when the citizen wants to report a cybercrime.

sections.title: Parent guidance for grooming and risky online contact
sections.text: The portal advises parents to discuss online threats such as grooming, bullying, and stalking with children, set clear boundaries for internet and online-game use, and pay attention when a child becomes unusually secretive or defensive about online activity. Help children choose strong privacy settings and tell a trusted adult about uncomfortable online contact.

sections.title: Young people: privacy, fake profiles, and stalking
sections.text: The portal recommends restricting social-media privacy settings, being selective about stranger requests, learning how to block an uncomfortable contact, and avoiding public sharing of personal details. For suspected cyberstalking, reduce location sharing, avoid sharing phone numbers, email addresses, and photographs with unknown people, and keep evidence of repeated unwanted contact.

sections.title: Safer devices and child sexual abuse material reporting
sections.text: The portal advises using passwords or device locks, keeping software updated, and installing apps only from trusted official sources. It says content relating to child sexual exploitative and abuse material should be reported to the relevant social-media service and can also be reported through the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal. Do not redistribute harmful content; preserve only the information needed for safe reporting.

sources.source_title: CERT-In Digital Safety Compass Handbook

sections.title: Phishing websites and links
sections.text: CERT-In advises treating unsolicited links and attachments cautiously. Verify shortened URLs before opening them, look for unusual spelling or grammar, use unique strong passwords, and never provide passwords or PINs by email or text. A real-looking website can still be designed to collect banking or personal information.

sections.title: Fake authority, digital arrest, and package threats
sections.text: CERT-In describes scams that use fake official calls, legal accusations, case numbers, package-seizure claims, and urgent threats to make people panic. Stay calm, verify a claim through an official channel, do not transfer money under pressure, and do not disclose payment or sensitive personal details to an unsolicited caller or message.

sections.title: Fake banking apps, phone scams, and remote access
sections.text: CERT-In warns that a message may push an APK or fake banking app in order to steal credentials or OTPs. Do not install banking apps from social media, text messages, or other unknown sources. For a caller claiming that a bank or service has a problem, contact the organisation through its official channel; do not share login or financial details and do not grant remote device access.

sections.title: Fake jobs, prizes, and emotional manipulation
sections.text: CERT-In lists common warning signs in fake jobs and prize offers: unexpected contact, unrealistically high income, pressure to act quickly, and requests for an upfront fee, account top-up, money transfer, or personal and banking details. Verify independently before committing money or information, and do not pay an advance fee to claim a job, reward, or prize.

sections.title: Payment, loan, and fake trading app scams
sections.text: CERT-In says a UPI PIN or OTP is not needed to receive money. Be cautious of urgent payment requests, unknown payment links, guaranteed loan offers, and trading apps promising high returns. Use an official app or website to verify a lender or registered broker, and do not transfer funds to a personal account because of an online investment promise.

sources.source_title: CERT-In Cyber Smart Kids: Suraksha Guide

sections.title: Children: protect personal information
sections.text: CERT-In advises children not to share their name, school, address, phone number, photographs, or other personal details online without a parent’s permission. Keep accounts private, accept requests only from people known offline, avoid unknown links and files, and tell a trusted adult if an online interaction feels frightening or wrong.

sections.title: Children: social-media privacy and location
sections.text: CERT-In recommends not publicly posting a school uniform, home, location, or routine, and avoiding public location tags and check-ins. Limit social-media visibility to people the child knows and ask a parent before posting personal material, because posts can be used for impersonation, tracking, or manipulation.

sections.title: Children: phishing and unsafe websites
sections.text: CERT-In says children should not click links from strangers, open unfamiliar files, or trust messages promising gifts, prizes, or urgent account warnings. Use trusted sites or bookmarks instead of searching for login pages, check addresses for unusual spelling, and tell a parent or teacher about a suspicious message.

sections.title: Children: grooming and cyberstalking
sections.text: CERT-In warns that strangers may build trust through games, chats, compliments, gifts, or secret requests before asking for photos or personal information. Do not respond to someone who causes discomfort, block and report the account where available, avoid sharing location or daily routine, and tell a trusted adult immediately.

sources.source_title: CERT-In Mahila Raksha: Cyber Safety for Women

sections.title: Digital footprint and location privacy
sections.text: CERT-In recommends thinking before posting because online material can be difficult to remove. Avoid sharing personal details, travel plans, daily routine, document images, or unnecessary live location. Keep social-media accounts private so that posts are visible only to trusted people.

sections.title: Passwords, multi-factor authentication, and urgent-message traps
sections.text: CERT-In advises long unique passwords, multi-factor authentication where available, and never sharing a password or OTP. Do not trust urgent messages asking for money or OTPs; verify the sender before following a link, expand and verify short URLs, and do not give banking or sensitive personal information by phone or online.

sections.title: Safe mobile apps and permissions
sections.text: CERT-In recommends locking a phone, downloading apps only from official app stores, applying updates, reviewing app permissions, and removing apps that are no longer used. Do not allow unnecessary access to contacts or the camera, especially when an app came from an untrusted source.

sources.source_title: CERT-In महिला रक्षा: हिंदी साइबर सुरक्षा सुझाव

sections.title: महिला सुरक्षा: डिजिटल निशान, OTP और संदिग्ध लिंक
sections.text: CERT-In के हिंदी महिला रक्षा सुझाव कहते हैं कि व्यक्तिगत जानकारी, यात्रा योजना, दैनिक दिनचर्या और अनावश्यक स्थान-साझाकरण को सार्वजनिक न करें। पैसे या OTP मांगने वाले अचानक संदेश पर भरोसा न करें, अज्ञात SMS या ई-मेल लिंक पर क्लिक न करें, और बैंकिंग या संवेदनशील जानकारी फोन अथवा ऑनलाइन किसी के साथ साझा न करें।

sources.source_title: CERT-In Cyber Security Awareness Booklet
sources.version: National Cyber Security Awareness Month 2023 booklet

sections.title: Vishing and fake customer-care contacts
sections.text: CERT-In warns that callers may pretend to be a bank, tax office, gas agency, or another trusted organisation and ask for card details or an OTP. Never share OTP, PIN, CVV, card details, or UPI PIN, including to receive money. Use customer-care details from an authorised website rather than numbers found randomly in search results, and review bank statements for irregularities.

sections.title: Malicious mobile apps and malware warning signs
sections.text: CERT-In advises downloading apps only from legitimate sites or authorised app stores, not from SMS, email, or social-media messages. Review requested permissions and user feedback before installing an app. Warning signs of malware can include unexpected pop-ups, redirection to suspicious sites, disabled security software, unexplained loss of storage, or messages sent from an account without permission.

sections.title: Social-media fraud, fake profiles, and child cyberbullying
sections.text: CERT-In recommends restricting public social-media visibility, verifying friend requests, using different passwords and multi-factor authentication, and never sharing social-media credentials. For a child facing bullying, stop engaging, save chats or messages, do not respond, block the contact, and tell a trusted parent, teacher, or elder.
retrieval_terms: my child is being bullied online

sections.title: Image misuse, blackmail, and support for women
sections.text: CERT-In describes image morphing and fake profiles as risks that can lead to harassment or blackmail. Preserve screenshots and other evidence, use privacy settings and strong multi-factor authentication, report an objectionable post or fake profile through the relevant social-media help centre, and seek support from trusted family or friends rather than suffering in silence.

sources.source_title: Reserve Bank of India: Increasing Instances of Payment Frauds

sections.title: Payment-fraud awareness: credentials, SIM swaps, links, and apps
sections.text: RBI’s payment-fraud awareness circular identifies common fraud patterns: requests for PINs, OTPs, or passwords; SIM-card swapping; links received in messages or email; and spurious apps that access information stored on a device. Treat these as warning signs, do not disclose critical payment information, and verify through the relevant bank or payment provider’s official channel.

sources.source_title: Reserve Bank of India: Customer Protection for Unauthorised Electronic Banking Transactions

sections.title: Promptly notify the bank about an unauthorised transaction
sections.text: RBI’s directions say customers should notify their bank as early as possible after an unauthorised electronic banking transaction and that banks must provide multiple 24x7 reporting channels. After receiving a report, banks must take immediate steps to prevent further unauthorised transactions. Exact liability and resolution outcomes depend on the applicable directions and the bank’s current policy, so Cyber Saathi must not promise a result.

sources.source_title: CERT-In Cyber Security Handbook for Women (Mahila Suraksha), March 2025

sections.title: Video calls from strangers, and intimate images
sections.text: CERT-In advises never merging with or responding to calls and video calls from unknown people, and verifying a caller identity first. It states that intimate pictures should never be shared over online video calls or social media with anybody, and warns that malicious mobile apps granted gallery or storage permission can read your photos, which can then be used to blackmail you. A PIN or OTP is never to be shared on a call or online.

sections.title: Morphing: what it is, and what to do
sections.text: CERT-In defines morphing as altering or changing the pictures of a person in photos or videos. Its guidance is to enable security and privacy features on social media, never post personal pictures publicly, and use multi-factor authentication with strong passwords. If it happens, save the evidence and screenshots for referring to the incident later, report a fake profile or objectionable post to that platform help centre, and do not suffer in silence - reach out to trusted family and friends.

sections.title: Cyberstalking: evidence and settings
sections.text: CERT-In advises taking screenshots of online messages, comments and conversations as proof, and noting down the mobile number and any available details of the person. Report the incident at cybercrime.gov.in or call 1930. To reduce exposure: do not accept friend requests from strangers, restrict social-media privacy to family and known friends, never post your home address or phone number, turn off location services on social platforms, and enable multi-factor authentication.

sections.title: Digital arrest scam
sections.text: CERT-In warns that cybercriminals pose as investigation officers and create fear through fake calls. Never agree to join an online video call for any investigation or arrest from a stranger, avoid answering video calls from unknown contacts even when they claim to know you, and never make a payment to anyone claiming to be an investigating officer on a call. Keep social-media privacy at the most restricted level. If you receive a call about an arrest or investigation, visit the nearest police station.

sections.title: Malicious APK files sent in chats
sections.text: CERT-In warns that fraudsters send malicious APK files through social-media messaging, and that clicking such links or installing files received in chats can lead to financial loss and theft of sensitive information. Malicious APKs target banking apps and steal financial data. Do not respond to messages asking for personal information or asking you to download an APK from a third-party website, install apps only from trusted sources rather than links sent in messages, and report fraud on 1930 or at cybercrime.gov.in.

sections.title: Instant loan app scams
sections.text: CERT-In advises availing loans only from RBI regulated entities and checking whether the lender is approved by RBI or associated with a financial institution. Download apps only from official websites and app stores, never enter a PIN or password anywhere in order to receive money, and check the terms of lending, the genuineness of the website, physical office location, Company Identification Number and Certificate of Registration. Check URLs and domain names in emails for spelling errors, and apply only through an authorised bank or NBFC application.

sections.title: Social media practice for women
sections.text: CERT-In advises blocking and reporting anyone causing trouble, both to the platform and to the concerned agencies. Set privacy so unauthorised people cannot view, chat with, or tag your content; be cautious accepting friend requests or replying to strangers; restrict visibility of posts and profile information; avoid sharing personal or sensitive details in posts or chats; and disable automatic addition to unknown groups. Keep a record of every online discomfort. If you become a victim of cyber fraud or cyber harassment, report at the nearest police station, at cybercrime.gov.in, or call 1930.

sections.title: Public Wi-Fi
sections.text: CERT-In advises confirming the network name and login procedure with staff before joining, and not conducting sensitive activity such as online shopping or banking over a public wireless network. Use public Wi-Fi only when required, switch Wi-Fi off when not in use, and be cautious connecting at airports, hotels, stations and cafes.

sections.title: Mobile app permissions
sections.text: CERT-In advises downloading apps only from official app stores and never from advertisements or third-party websites, keeping the operating system and applications updated, reading reviews of the app and developer first, and reviewing permission requests to check they relate to the purpose of the app. Remove apps with excessive permissions, uninstall apps no longer used, and restrict permissions to social media and banking accounts. Report unauthorised activity to the concerned authorities immediately.

sections.title: Reporting a cyber security incident to CERT-In
sections.text: Separately from a police complaint, CERT-In is the national agency for incident response under Section 70B of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Cyber security incidents can be reported to CERT-In by email at incident@cert-in.org.in, through its website cert-in.org.in, or on the toll-free number 1800-11-4949. This is a technical incident-response channel and does not replace a complaint on the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal or the 1930 helpline.

sources.source_title: CERT-In Internet Safety Awareness Booklet for Digital Nagriks
sources.version: Safer Internet Day booklet, 6 February 2024, reviewed 2026-09-12

sections.title: Aadhaar: locking biometrics and using a Virtual ID
sections.text: CERT-In advises locking your biometrics through the m-Aadhaar app or the UIDAI portal to prevent unauthorised access to your account details, and using a Virtual ID or Masked Aadhaar so the Aadhaar number itself is not disclosed. Link Aadhaar to your mobile number so you are alerted to activity, keep digital copies secure, never share Aadhaar details or an OTP with strangers, and avoid saving a digital Aadhaar on a public computer - delete any copies from a public machine once your work is done.

sections.title: Online shopping safety
sections.text: CERT-In advises shopping only on trusted websites and verifying the genuineness of the brand and the e-commerce site, and verifying genuineness before paying by card. Check that the site is secured - https or a padlock in the address bar - keep track of your digital payments, and check you are paying for the right product. Never respond to emails asking for personal information or account details, avoid public Wi-Fi for financial transactions, and do not click suspicious links offering discounts or prizes that seem too good to be true.

sections.title: Social media exposure
sections.text: CERT-In advises against sharing an address, mobile number, personal email or other identity information on social media, and against posting personal pictures publicly. Never accept friend requests without verification, never click a suspicious link or download an app received in a message until the source is verified, use different passwords for different accounts, enable multi-factor authentication, disable profile visibility from public searches, and log out after each session. Criminals can collect enough information about someone from their posts and profile alone.

sections.title: Mobile phone safety
sections.text: CERT-In advises downloading apps only from the Play Store or App Store and never from third-party websites or links received in messages or chats, enabling only the permissions an app actually needs, and never sharing an OTP received for any application with anyone. Keep the operating system and anti-malware software updated, keep the phone locked when not in use, do not click suspicious links from strangers, and avoid USB charging in public places.

sections.title: Recognising a suspicious email or message
sections.text: CERT-In advises avoiding links and attachments from unknown sources, not filling in forms that arrive by unsolicited email, and not clicking links in emails from untrusted sources. It names urgency as a warning sign in itself: an email or message that creates a sense of urgency should be treated with suspicion. Scan the system regularly with updated anti-malware software.

sections.title: Checking a link before opening it
sections.text: CERT-In advises expanding shortened URLs and verifying them before clicking, checking that a website address carries https or a padlock icon, disabling pop-up windows, clearing browser cookies and cache regularly, turning Safe Search on, and disabling the browser option that remembers logins and passwords.

sources.source_title: CERT-In Cyber Security Handbook, National Cyber Security Awareness Month 2024

sections.title: Verifying the sender of an email
sections.text: CERT-In advises verifying the sender before clicking any link or attachment, and checking the domain name in the sender address for misspellings or typos - a near-identical domain is the common trick. Do not click links or attachments in suspicious emails from strangers, do not use an official email account for online shopping or ticket booking, do not open shortened URLs from email or chat without expanding them first, and never store usernames and passwords on a public system.

sections.title: Passwords after a compromise
sections.text: CERT-In advises long passwords, because short ones are easy to crack, and warns that dictionary words are vulnerable to brute-force attack. Mix uppercase, lowercase, numerals and special characters, avoid guessable patterns, change passwords periodically, never reuse a password across accounts, and enable multi-factor authentication so a stolen password alone is not enough.

sections.title: Backups before and after an incident
sections.text: CERT-In advises taking regular backups of important files and data, because after hardware failure or a cyberattack a backup is what allows information to be restored. Keep multiple copies in different locations so one disaster cannot take them all, and periodically test and verify the backups so they are known to work when they are actually needed.

sources.source_title: Sanchar Saathi, Department of Telecommunications citizen-centric services

sections.title: Chakshu: report the number that called or messaged you
sections.text: Chakshu on the Department of Telecommunications Sanchar Saathi portal is where a citizen reports a suspected fraud communication - a call, SMS or WhatsApp message sent with the intention of cyber-crime, financial fraud or impersonation. Go to sancharsaathi.gov.in, open Citizen Centric Services, choose Chakshu, select the medium the message arrived on and the category of fraud, enter the details of the communication, verify your own mobile number by OTP, and submit. Chakshu acts on the telecom connection itself, which is a different remedy from a police complaint: if money was lost or a crime has occurred, that is still reported on 1930 or at cybercrime.gov.in.
retrieval_terms: report the number that called me
where do I report a number

sections.title: TAFCOP: how many SIM cards are registered on your name
sections.text: A mobile connection taken on someone else identity documents is how many frauds are run, and the person whose name it is on usually never finds out. The Department of Telecommunications publishes this at tafcop.sancharsaathi.gov.in: log in with your mobile number and an OTP and the portal lists every mobile connection issued against your name. Any connection you do not recognise can be marked as not your number, and one you no longer want as not required. On a reported connection outgoing services are suspended within 30 days and the connection is disconnected within 60 days.

sections.title: Calls from abroad showing an Indian number, and unwanted commercial calls
sections.text: Many fraud calls originate outside India but are made to display a +91 Indian number. The Department of Telecommunications takes these reports through the Report Incoming International Call with Indian Number service on Sanchar Saathi - enter the number you received the call from with the date and time and verify by OTP - or on the helplines 1963 and 1800-110-420. Unwanted promotional calls and SMS are a separate matter and are reported as Unsolicited Commercial Communication, either through Chakshu or to 1909 by call or SMS, or on the TRAI DND app.

sections.title: Checking whether the caller really is your bank or a government office
sections.text: Sanchar Saathi publishes a Trusted Contact Details directory: the authentic phone numbers and websites of banks, financial institutions and government agencies, searchable by the name of the institution, by a phone number, or by a website address. If someone has called claiming to be from your bank or from a government department, the number they called from can be checked against this directory before you act on anything they said. A number that does not appear there is not proof of fraud by itself, but a caller pressing you to pay or to share an OTP is.

sources.source_title: CEIR - Central Equipment Identity Register, blocking a lost or stolen mobile

sections.title: Phone lost or stolen: blocking the handset itself
sections.text: A lost or stolen phone carries the banking apps, the OTPs and the logged-in accounts, so blocking the handset matters as much as blocking the SIM. The Department of Telecommunications CEIR service at ceir.gov.in blocks the handset by its IMEI across every network in India, so it cannot be used with another SIM. The order is: file a police report and keep a copy, get a duplicate SIM for the lost number from your operator because the request is verified by OTP on that number - SMS works about 24 hours after the new SIM is activated - then submit the blocking request on ceir.gov.in with the police report and an identity proof, and keep the Request ID it returns. The handset is blocked within 24 hours. If the phone is later recovered, report the recovery to the police and submit the un-blocking form; if the block was registered through the State Police, the un-blocking is done through them.

sources.source_title: Grievance Appellate Committee, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
sources.version: constituted under the IT Rules 2021, reviewed 2026-09-12

sections.title: The platform refused to remove the content: appealing that decision
sections.text: When a social media platform rejects a report, or simply never replies, that is not the end of it. The Grievance Appellate Committee, set up by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under the Information Technology Rules, 2021, hears appeals from users against the decision of a platform Grievance Officer. The appeal is filed online at gac.gov.in, and the whole process from filing to decision is digital. There is one precondition and one deadline: you must have complained to the platform own Grievance Officer first, and the appeal must be filed within 30 days of their reply - or within 30 days of the date you should have received a reply and did not.

sections.title: What the Grievance Appellate Committee does not handle
sections.text: The Grievance Appellate Committee decides complaints about a platform handling of content and about the computer resources it makes available. It does not handle financial fraud or cybercrime: those are directed to the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal at cybercrime.gov.in or to the 1930 helpline. The two paths run in parallel and one does not replace the other - a person whose morphed photograph is still online after the platform refused to act can have a police complaint on NCRP and an appeal before the Committee at the same time.

sources.source_title: RBI Financial Awareness Messages (FAME), Financial Inclusion and Development Department

sections.title: What the bank owes you after an unauthorised transaction
sections.text: RBI states that whoever is at fault, you must notify your bank immediately when you find a fraudulent or unauthorised electronic banking transaction on your account or card, because the longer you take the larger the loss. The bank has to give you an acknowledgement for that complaint. It must credit the disputed amount back to your account within 10 working days of your notification, and it must resolve the complaint within 90 days. If fraudulent transactions continue after you informed the bank, the bank bears that loss.

sections.title: Zero liability: why reporting within three days matters so much
sections.text: RBI sets out when the customer bears nothing at all. If there is no negligence by you and you inform the bank within 3 working days of the unauthorised transaction, you have zero liability. You also have zero liability where the fault was the bank - a deficiency in the bank system - whether or not you reported it. In a third-party breach, where the fault is neither yours nor the bank but elsewhere in the system, reporting within 3 working days again means zero liability. If the loss was due to your own negligence, such as sharing a password, PIN or OTP, you bear the loss only up to the point you inform the bank - which is why reporting late is the expensive mistake, not reporting at all.
retrieval_terms: do I still lose the money
will I get my money back

sections.title: If you report late: the capped amounts
sections.text: RBI caps the customer loss even when the report is delayed. Where the fault lies neither with the bank nor with the customer but elsewhere in the system, and the customer takes four to seven working days after the bank communication to notify it, the liability per transaction is the transaction value or the cap below, whichever is lower. The cap is Rs 5,000 for BSBD (basic savings) accounts. It is Rs 10,000 for all other savings accounts, for pre-paid payment instruments and gift cards, for current, cash-credit and overdraft accounts of MSMEs, for such accounts of individuals with an annual average balance up to Rs 25 lakh, and for credit cards with a limit up to Rs 5 lakh. It is Rs 25,000 for all other current, cash-credit and overdraft accounts and for credit cards with a limit above Rs 5 lakh.

sections.title: When the bank does not resolve it: the RBI Ombudsman, free of cost
sections.text: RBI runs a cost-free escalation above the bank. You must complain to the bank, NBFC, payment system participant or credit information company first. If that complaint is not redressed within 30 days, or no reply comes, or the reply does not satisfy you, you can then lodge a complaint with the RBI Ombudsman - online at cms.rbi.org.in, or by post to the Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre, 4th Floor, Reserve Bank of India, Sector-17, Central Vista, Chandigarh-160017. There is no fee, and no third party or agency is needed; filing on the CMS portal gives an instant acknowledgement and a complaint number. The complaint must include evidence that you approached the bank and did not get a satisfactory response, and it cannot be one already pending in a court or already settled by the Ombudsman. A complaint cannot be filed through an advocate.

sections.title: UPI: safe use and the two rules that stop most UPI losses
sections.text: RBI describes UPI as transfer between two bank accounts from a smartphone, set up once using the debit card linked to the account, and used thereafter with a UPI PIN. Its stated Dos are to keep the UPI app updated, to always review a merchant or person collect request before accepting it, and to recheck and reconfirm the amount and the beneficiary before transferring. Its Don'ts are two: never share your PIN with anyone, and do not transfer money without verifying and reconfirming the recipient first. A UPI PIN is needed to send money, never to receive it - a collect request accepted carelessly takes money out.

sections.title: Online and mobile banking: what RBI tells customers to do
sections.text: RBI advises typing the bank URL yourself using only verified and trusted browsers and HTTPS secured sites, and never reaching your bank website through an online search. Use passwords that are hard to guess with alphanumeric and special characters and change them frequently, keep payment apps updated, and link your mobile number and email to the account with SMS and email alerts switched on so an unusual transaction is visible at once. Never store login credentials on your phone or enter them on untrusted portals, avoid transacting from public devices, cyber cafes and open or free public Wi-Fi, and never share a mobile banking PIN, internet banking ID, password or OTP. Inform the bank immediately about any unusual or unauthorised transaction.

sections.title: ATM and card: skimming, and a failed ATM transaction
sections.text: RBI advises using an EMV chip-and-PIN debit card rather than a magnetic strip card, checking for unauthorised cameras or skimming devices near the ATM, covering the keypad with one hand while entering the PIN, counting the notes dispensed, and collecting the card afterwards. Register your phone number with the card-issuing bank for transaction alerts, and contact the bank immediately to block the card if it is lost or stolen or you believe it is compromised. Never share card number, expiry, CVV, PIN or OTP, never leave the card in the machine, and never write the PIN on the card. A failed ATM transaction - money debited but not dispensed - must be raised with the card-issuing bank immediately: banks must resolve it within T+5 days or pay you compensation of Rs 100 per day of delay.

sections.title: Loan apps and investment schemes: checking before, reporting after
sections.text: RBI states that a digital lending app must be associated with an RBI-regulated bank or NBFC, and that you can check this on that bank or NBFC own website before installing. Do not download a loan app from a link received over SMS or social media. Read the Key Fact Statement, sanction letter and privacy policy, confirm the documents are digitally signed and on the letterhead of the bank or NBFC, and check what permissions the app demands before installing. A suspicious loan app, whether on an app store or arriving as a link, should be reported to law enforcement agencies. For deposits and investments, RBI says to place money only with entities registered with or regulated by RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA or the Government, and to report any entity that has defaulted on repayment at sachet.rbi.org.in.

sections.title: Lottery, prize and fake-RBI messages
sections.text: RBI states plainly that RBI and banks never ask for your bank account, credit card or debit card details, PIN or OTP through email, SMS or phone calls, and that RBI does not open savings, current or fixed deposit accounts for individuals, does not issue credit or debit cards, and does not transact with any individual. So a message saying you have won a lottery whose money is deposited with RBI, or asking for account details to release a prize, is fraudulent on its face. If someone promises free money or a prize for a ticket you never bought, pause and ask why. RBI sends its own awareness SMS from the sender ID RBISAY, and its public awareness line is 14440.

sources.source_title: CERT-In Cyber Security Best Practices for Senior Citizens, October 2025
sources.version: National Cyber Security Awareness Month 2025 booklet, reviewed 2026-09-12

sections.title: Vishing: the fraud call that sounds like your bank
sections.text: CERT-In uses the word vishing for a scam call, where the caller pretends to be a bank official. Its guidance: never share an OTP, PIN, CVV or debit and credit card details with anyone, and do not respond to any call asking for bank account or card details or other sensitive information. Do not give personal information in order to receive a prize, lottery, gift or KYC update. Use only the customer-care numbers published on the authorised website of the bank or organisation, not a number given to you on the call. Hang up immediately if the caller pressures you or creates panic, and report the suspicious call to your bank and to the authorities.

sections.title: Smishing: the fraud SMS
sections.text: CERT-In uses the word smishing for fraud by SMS - fake bank alerts, lottery and prize messages, KYC update requests, government impersonation, and messages carrying malicious links or attachments. Its guidance: avoid clicking unfamiliar links received in messages because they can steal personal data from the phone, always verify the message is authentic, and never share an OTP, PIN or password over SMS. Banks and government bodies do not ask for sensitive information by SMS. Spelling mistakes and poor grammar are signs of a fraudulent message. Do not reply to unknown numbers or engage with prize and lottery claims - check any account or service update in the official app or website instead.

sections.title: Quishing: fraud through a QR code
sections.text: CERT-In uses the word quishing for fraud through QR codes - fake payment QR codes, phishing via QR codes, malware downloads, and scams run from QR codes on public posters. Its guidance: do not scan QR codes sent by strangers in chats or emails. Before scanning, check that the code is legitimate and has not been altered or covered with a fraudulent sticker - a sticker pasted over a shop genuine code is the common trick. Do not enter personal or banking details on a website opened through a QR code, avoid scanning codes on public posters or flyers unless verified, and examine the URL the scanner shows before opening it.

sections.title: Safe online banking for people who bank on a phone
sections.text: CERT-In lists the threats to online banking as phishing websites that steal login credentials, fraudulent apps that mimic real banking apps, vishing calls and smishing messages. Its practices: use only verified and trusted browsers and HTTPS secured sites for payments, never share an online banking PIN or OTP, enable multi-factor authentication, log out after every banking session, change the password regularly, keep payment apps updated to the latest version, and avoid banking over public Wi-Fi. Keep a regular check on every message the bank sends, and if something looks wrong contact the bank immediately on its official customer-care number.

sections.title: Threats aimed at older people, and what to do if it happens
sections.text: CERT-In names the threats older people meet most often as phishing messages, courier fraud, financial frauds and emotional manipulation. Its mobile practices are a strong screen lock, never sharing OTPs, PINs or passwords with strangers, keeping software updated, downloading apps only from official app stores, verifying the source before clicking a link, reviewing app permissions, avoiding public Wi-Fi, turning Bluetooth and location off when unused, and treating fake update alerts and pop-ups with suspicion. If you do become a victim, CERT-In says to call 1930 immediately and report the fraud at cybercrime.gov.in.

sources.source_title: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021

sections.title: The law gives the platform 24 hours to remove an intimate or morphed image
sections.text: Rule 3(2)(b) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 requires an intermediary - a social media platform, a messaging service, a website that hosts user content - to act within twenty-four hours of receiving a complaint about content that, on the face of it, exposes a person's private area, shows them in full or partial nudity, shows or depicts them in a sexual act or conduct, or is impersonation in electronic form including an artificially morphed image of that person. Within that twenty-four hours the platform must take all reasonable and practicable measures to remove the content or disable access to it. The complaint can be made by the individual concerned or by any person on their behalf, so a parent, a friend or a helpline can file it. Rule 3(2)(c) requires the platform to provide a mechanism for making exactly this kind of complaint.

sections.title: The platform's Grievance Officer, and the clock they are on
sections.text: Rule 3(2)(a) requires every intermediary to prominently publish the name and contact details of its Grievance Officer, and the mechanism by which a user or a victim can complain - on the home page or home screen, or on a page directly reachable from it. That officer must acknowledge a complaint within twenty-four hours and resolve it within fifteen days. Where the complaint is a request to remove content or a communication link falling under rule 3(1)(b), it must be acted on as expeditiously as possible and resolved within seventy-two hours. So a report that goes unanswered past these deadlines is not just ignored, it is a breach of the rule - and that is what makes an appeal available.

sections.title: Evidence the platform must keep after it removes something
sections.text: A common fear is that getting content taken down destroys the proof needed for the police case. Rule 3(1)(g) answers it: where an intermediary has removed information or disabled access to it, it must preserve that information and the associated records for one hundred and eighty days for investigation purposes, without vitiating the evidence in any manner, and longer if a court or a lawfully authorised government agency requires. Rule 3(1)(j) requires the intermediary to provide information in its control, or assistance, to a lawfully authorised government agency within seventy-two hours of receiving an order. Reporting content for removal and preserving evidence are therefore not in conflict - but your own screenshots are still worth keeping, because they are what you can produce yourself.

sections.title: Appealing to the Grievance Appellate Committee: the rule and the deadlines
sections.text: Rule 3A establishes the Grievance Appellate Committees. Under rule 3A(3), a person aggrieved by a decision of a platform's Grievance Officer - or whose grievance was not resolved within the period rule 3(2) allows - may appeal within thirty days of receiving the Grievance Officer's communication. The Committee is to try to decide the appeal within thirty calendar days of receiving it, and under rule 3A(6) the entire process from filing to decision is conducted online. Rule 3A(7) is the part that gives the decision teeth: every order passed by the Committee must be complied with by the intermediary, and a report to that effect uploaded on its website. Appeals are filed at gac.gov.in.

sections.title: Large platforms carry extra duties, including a 24x7 police contact
sections.text: Rule 4(1) places additional duties on a significant social media intermediary - the large platforms. It must appoint a Chief Compliance Officer resident in India who is responsible for compliance with the Act and these rules and can be held liable for a failure of due diligence; a nodal contact person resident in India for 24x7 coordination with law enforcement agencies, to ensure their lawful orders and requisitions are complied with; and a Resident Grievance Officer, who performs the grievance functions under rule 3(2). This is why a police complaint on the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal can move faster than a user report alone: the investigating officer has a named, round-the-clock channel into the platform that a member of the public does not.

sources.source_title: Information Security Education and Awareness (ISEA), MeitY and C-DAC

sections.title: Romance scam: befriended online, then asked for money
sections.text: ISEA describes an online romance scam as a fraudster using a fake profile to build a relationship and then persuading the victim to part with money on some pretext - an emergency, an accident or hospitalisation, a bogus scheme, or an investment opportunity presented with urgency. The money is asked for through gift cards, UPI, bank transfer or reloadable cards, and once enough has been extracted the person disappears. The warning signs it lists: affection expressed very early, being unusually empathetic and obliging, always avoiding meeting in person, details that do not match when checked, and requests for money or gifts. Intimate pictures shared during the relationship may later be used to extort more. ISEA advises never sending money to someone met online, never sharing banking details or identity documents, keeping a neutral person informed who can assess the interaction, ending the relationship if you suspect a scam, reporting the profile on the platform, approaching the bank if any banking details were shared, and filing at cybercrime.gov.in or the nearest cybercrime cell.

sections.title: Matrimonial fraud: a profile that looked respectable
sections.text: ISEA treats fraud through matrimonial sites as a distinct pattern: a profile claiming a respectable position and family, pursued with the family's approval, followed some time later by a request for money in dire need - after which the person becomes untraceable. Its guidance is to check the authenticity of the matrimonial site before registering and to use a separate email address for it; not to publish your mobile number or residential address openly on the profile; never to share private pictures, bank account details or identity documents with someone recently met; to take ample time over a thorough background check, with professional help if needed; to be especially cautious with an overseas profile; and to meet in person in a public place and ask enough questions before proceeding.

sections.title: SIM swap: the phone goes dead and then the account is emptied
sections.text: ISEA explains SIM swapping - also called SIM splitting, SIM jacking or SIM hijacking - as a fraudster getting your mobile number registered on a SIM card they hold, which hands them your OTPs, PINs and authentication SMS, and through those your bank and social accounts even without your passwords. It happens in three ways: the fraudster impersonates you to the operator and requests a port to a new SIM claiming the phone was lost, stolen or broken; or uses a fake ID to get the existing SIM blocked and the number reissued; or calls you posing as a service-provider executive offering a better plan or coverage, gets you to read out the 20-digit number printed on your SIM, and then has you press 1 to authorise the swap. The signs that matter, because they arrive before the money goes: being unable to make calls or send messages, no mobile signal for an extended period, being unable to log in to your apps, and social accounts being hacked. Treat a sudden unexplained loss of signal as urgent - contact the operator at once rather than waiting for it to come back.

sections.title: Fake tech support and remote-access apps
sections.text: ISEA describes tech support fraud as criminals posing as customer, security or technical support staff. A pop-up or blue screen warns that the device is infected, sometimes with alarming audio and a list of supposedly dangerous files, and will not close; it urges you to call a toll-free number or click a link. The aim is to frighten you into paying for repairs or software, and to get remote access to your device. Its warning signs: an unsolicited call or email from someone claiming to be a well-known technology company, since those companies do not contact customers unless the customer started it; a warning that urges you to call a number immediately; bad grammar; and being asked to pay by gift card, cash-reload card or wire transfer. Do not grant remote access to your computer or phone. Searching online for a toll-free support number is itself risky, because the results can lead to another fraudster - go to the website of the company or the retailer you bought from instead.

sections.title: How OTP frauds are actually run
sections.text: ISEA sets out the pretexts used to get an OTP out of someone: free gifts, offers and discounts, easy loans, a call from a supposed online shopping executive, KYC updation, a credit limit enhancement, or a food delivery executive. One common script: the caller says an order is out for delivery, and when you say you did not place it, sends a link to cancel it and asks for the OTP to confirm the cancellation - the OTP then authorises a payment. ISEA advises that no genuine service provider ever asks a customer for an OTP, CVV or PIN; not clicking links in messages from unknown sources; not filling forms reached from such links; checking your messages so that an OTP generated without your knowledge is noticed immediately; never installing screen-sharing apps at anyone's suggestion; not using contact numbers found through a search engine; and disposing of old passbooks, cheque books and Aadhaar copies properly rather than handing photocopies to strangers. If it happens, inform the service provider, block the card, and report at cybercrime.gov.in or on 1930.

sections.title: KYC fraud: the message or call saying your account will be blocked
sections.text: ISEA describes KYC fraud in two forms. On a call, the fraudster poses as a bank or e-wallet representative, warns that the account will be blocked or suspended unless KYC is updated immediately, has you download an app, asks you to share a code and grant permissions - which gives them your device - and then asks you to transfer a small amount, which lets them see the OTP and the credentials they need to empty the account. By message, a phishing link leads to a spoofed bank site asking for username, password and OTP, or a 10-digit mobile number is given to call. Its warning signs: a request for confidential information, a request to install an app, manufactured urgency, poor grammar and odd capitalisation, and a message from a plain mobile number rather than a registered bank sender ID. Two rules it states plainly: banks and wallet companies never do KYC over a call or by sending links, and a genuine customer-care number is never a 10-digit mobile number.

sections.title: AePS: money taken using a fingerprint, without any OTP
sections.text: The Aadhaar Enabled Payment System lets a person withdraw or deposit cash, check a balance and transfer funds through a banking correspondent using their Aadhaar number and a fingerprint, at a micro-ATM or Aadhaar-enabled POS machine. ISEA notes the point that matters after a fraud: AePS requires no OTP and no PIN, so a victim may see money leave the account with no message asking them to approve anything. It names the risks - a fingerprint can be copied with glue in what is called the gummy-finger method, far more easily than a card can be cloned, and a merchant's device or phone may retain the biometric data captured. Its practices: verify the Aadhaar number before any transfer, use Aadhaar only at a proper POS and biometric capture device, and check that the device is certified and has not been tampered with. The transaction limit is Rs 50,000 per account per day.

sections.title: Buying or selling on a classified marketplace
sections.text: ISEA describes the scams run on online classified marketplaces from both sides. Against a seller: a supposed buyer claims to be far away or abroad, promises to cover shipping, and sends a representative from a courier service who is part of the scam to collect the item and the shipping charges; fake courier paperwork and a fake email, sometimes appearing to come from a bank asking for courier details before releasing the money, keep the seller believing the deal is real, and neither the payment nor the shipping money ever arrives. Against a buyer: fake ads copy the pictures and details of a genuine listing and price the item far below comparable ones to create a hurry. Common to both: the other party refuses to meet or speak on the phone and communicates only by message, pushes payment by prepaid card, UPI, net banking, cryptocurrency or a money transfer service, asks for personal and financial details to prove you are genuine, or proposes meeting alone in a secluded place.

sections.title: Sextortion: threatened with an intimate video or photo
sections.text: ISEA describes online sextortion as a fraudster threatening to circulate your private material unless you provide more images, sexual favours or money, sometimes also threatening your friends or relatives using information taken from your devices. The approach comes through messaging apps, dating apps, social platforms or adult sites; the fraudster records the video call, takes screenshots, or morphs pictures that were sent, and then begins blackmailing. Warning signs of an attempt: repeated messages or video calls from unknown numbers, repeated friend requests, repeated requests for intimate pictures or video chats, conversation steered toward intimate topics, and a rush to build intimacy. ISEA's guidance if it has happened: save the evidence and screenshots, use the platform's Report User option, do not suffer in silence but reach out to trusted family and friends, and file a complaint at a cybercrime cell or online - noting explicitly that such a complaint can be filed anonymously on the national cybercrime reporting portal. It also names the signs of a victim in distress: fear, anxiety, depression, withdrawal, and suicidal or self-harming thoughts.

sections.title: Intimate images shared after a relationship ended
sections.text: ISEA covers the case where private images or videos are published by someone who was trusted with them. Its guidance before it happens: be cautious about sharing or allowing intimate pictures because relationships may turn sour, do not continue with anyone who pressures you to share them, and do not forward anyone else's - forwarding is a breach of trust and can itself be a serious crime. After it happens: register a complaint online at cybercrime.gov.in, where such crimes can be registered anonymously, or at the nearest cybercrime police station. On the law, ISEA identifies the Information Technology Act provisions that apply - section 66E on violation of privacy, sections 67 and 67A on publishing or transmitting obscene and sexually explicit material in electronic form, and section 72 on breach of confidentiality and privacy - together with the Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986, which prohibits publishing indecent representation of women.

sections.title: Doxxing: your address and number posted to invite harassment
sections.text: ISEA defines doxxing as someone publishing your personal information - address, telephone number and the like - online, openly inviting others to harass you with it, often alongside false accusations. Its effect is an invasion of privacy and a humiliating, socially damaging experience, and the signs in a person affected are anxiety, depression, strong reactions and mood swings, anxiety on checking the phone, and withdrawing or becoming secretive. Its guidance: do not publish your address, mobile number or personal email openly, use two-factor authentication with different strong passwords on each account, and save the evidence and screenshots for referring to the incident later. Action: register a complaint at the nearest cybercrime police station or online at cybercrime.gov.in, which can be done anonymously, and report it to the platform's help centre.

sections.title: Online trolling, and the evidence a social-media complaint needs
sections.text: ISEA describes trolling as posting inflammatory, abusive or offensive messages meant to provoke an emotional reaction, and warns it can lead to depression and self-harm. Its guidance: stay calm and block rather than reacting, complain to the platform's help centre immediately, restrict your privacy settings, and share videos privately. It then lists what a social-media complaint should have ready, which applies to online abuse generally: a copy or screenshot of the content, pictures, comments, messages and profile; a screenshot of the URL of that content; the material in both hard and soft form; and a copy of the complaint you made to the platform's help centre. Note the mobile number and any other details of the person. Always save screenshots as proof before anything is deleted.

sections.title: Cyber flashing: obscene images sent by a stranger
sections.text: ISEA describes cyber flashing as a form of online harassment in which unsolicited sexual or obscene images are sent over a messaging app or by a phone's nearby-sharing feature - and notes that nearby-sharing means the sender may be physically close to you. Its practical steps: turn the nearby-sharing or AirDrop receiving setting off; do not accept video calls from unknown numbers; do not open images or videos received from unknown numbers; turn off automatic media download in your messaging app so such content is not saved to your phone; set a screen lock and enable the phone's privacy features; and disable location services, including location permission for individual apps, when posting online. Save a screenshot as evidence first. A complaint can be filed at the nearest cybercrime police station or online at cybercrime.gov.in, anonymously if you prefer.

sections.title: Online grooming: how a child is drawn in, stage by stage
sections.text: ISEA sets out grooming as a slow, deliberate process rather than a single incident, which is why parents often miss it. The stages it names: the perpetrator targets a child, choosing one who seems emotionally needy, isolated, neglected or without much parental oversight, and gives them special attention; gains trust, including the parents' trust, by learning what the child needs and providing it; fills that need with gifts, money, flattery and affection; isolates the child by creating situations where they are alone and by cultivating the sense that only the groomer truly understands them, more than the parents do; then progressively sexualises the relationship through talk, pictures and situations involving nakedness; and finally maintains control through secrecy, blame and threats to keep the child silent. Groomers use fake accounts and photos and often pose as a child of the same age with the same hobbies, and may move the conversation off a game or platform somewhere more private. They may also use help inside a game to obtain a family member's card details. A child often does not understand they are being groomed.

sections.title: Fake job offers
sections.text: ISEA describes fake job offers reaching people who have applied for jobs online: the fraudster collects the details posted on job sites and sends emails that appear to come from genuine companies through fake mailer services, sometimes conducting an interview and sending an offer letter, and spoofing calls in the name of a large company. Money is demanded before and after the offer letter, deposited into various bank accounts and withdrawn at once. Its precautions: do not respond to such mail without verifying where it came from, do not deposit money unless the candidate has been interviewed in person by the company, check the company's own website for any such job opening before proceeding, and do not try to obtain a job by paying for it.

sections.title: Where you can file, and what to do if the police will not take it
sections.text: ISEA states that under the Information Technology Act a cyber crime comes under global jurisdiction, which means a cyber crime complaint can be registered with any cyber cell in India regardless of where the offence was actually committed - you are not sent back to the city where the fraudster was. Most cities now have a dedicated cyber crime cell. The written complaint is addressed to the Head of the Cyber Crime Cell of the city you are in, and carries your name, contact details and address for mailing. If you cannot reach a cyber cell, a First Information Report can be filed at the local police station. And if the complaint is not accepted there, ISEA says you can approach the Commissioner of Police or the city's Judicial Magistrate - refusal at the counter is not the end of the road. Separately, a cyber security incident can be reported to CERT-In, the national nodal agency under section 70B of the IT Act.

sections.title: 1098: the child helpline, and reporting child sexual abuse material
sections.text: ISEA defines online child pornography as the abuse or exploitation of a minor under 18 in a sexually explicit act or conduct online, through images or videos, and describes predators using social media, gaming sites and chat rooms to lure children into such situations. Its guidance to a child or young person: if an online contact is unusually attentive, claims all the same interests, and pushes to meet in person, that is a warning sign; never agree to meet someone befriended online without telling your parents; and if anything makes you uncomfortable, cut off contact, tell your parents and report it. Such content can be reported to the platform and at cybercrime.gov.in, and the child helpline 1098, run under the Ministry of Women and Child Development, can be contacted. The signs in a child who has been affected are guilt, shame, distress, withdrawal and depression.

sections.title: What the law guarantees a child victim under POCSO
sections.text: Families often do not report abuse of a child because they fear the child being exposed, and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 is written against exactly that fear. ISEA sets out its protections: the Act is gender neutral, applying to girls and boys alike; penetrative and non-penetrative sexual assault are each defined; the trial is held in camera and in special courts; disclosing the identity of a victim is itself an offence punishable with imprisonment; the child's statement is to be recorded by a woman police officer at the child's residence or another place of the child's convenience, rather than at a police station; and compensation to the child victim can be awarded from the assets of the accused. Child pornography and cyber bullying of children also attract sections 66 and 67 of the Information Technology Act.

sections.title: Cyberbullying, and the signs in a child who is being bullied
sections.text: ISEA describes cyber bullying as intimidating online behaviour on a public platform - threatening, humiliating, embarrassing or harassing posts, teasing, rumours spread by email or on social networks, unwanted messages, defamation, and embarrassing pictures, videos or fake profiles. It happens through phones, computers and tablets and through social media, text messages, email, chat rooms and discussion groups. Its warning that matters most to a parent is what a bullied child looks like rather than what the bullying looks like: recurrent health complaints and eating poorly, avoiding school or college, isolating themselves, appearing depressed, sad, worried or agitated, and losing interest in activities. It notes that the harm runs to social isolation, mental stress and suicidal attempts, so these signs are not something to wait out.

sections.title: Sexting between teenagers, and why forwarding it is serious
sections.text: ISEA describes sexting as sharing sexually explicit images or videos over the internet or through phones, and notes it is not a one-sided phenomenon - girls and boys take part about equally, which matters because the assumption that boys ask and girls send shapes how families react. The consequences it names are real: images forwarded to people they were never meant for cause serious emotional distress, and sexting between a minor under 18 and an adult falls under child pornography law whether or not the images were shared willingly - for the person sending and the person receiving. Its advice to parents is to raise it early and repeatedly, not to turn it into a conversation about morals, to discuss the unwanted distribution and the legal consequences plainly, and to make clear that no one has to prove love this way.

sections.title: Someone made a fake profile in your name
sections.text: ISEA describes fake profile creation as a fraudster building a social media profile from your identity details - name, address, email, photograph - without your knowledge, in order to harm you. What they do with it: spread false information, damage your reputation, send friend requests to your actual friends and family so those people can be phished or defrauded in turn, lure children and teenagers behind your identity, and ask your contacts for money or gifts. Profiles of army personnel, well-known people and professionals working abroad are common templates. Its guidance: do not publish high-resolution personal pictures publicly, prefer group photographs over individual ones, keep address, mobile number and personal email off the profile, use a different password for each account with two-factor authentication, and be alert to anyone asking you about online activity you do not recognise - that is often the first sign. Report the fake profile both to the platform and at cybercrime.gov.in.

sections.title: Fake government subsidy and scheme messages
sections.text: ISEA warns about messages and links spread through instant messaging apps and social media offering government subsidies, schemes, grants and cash offers. The pattern: you receive the link, you are prompted to click it, register, or take a survey, and you are redirected to a malicious site - which leads to a data leak, malware, siphoned money or a hacked account. Its warning signs are a tweaked website address, a generic message that does not use your name, a request for personal details unrelated to the supposed scheme, and an offer that sounds too good to be true. Verify any such announcement on the official government website itself rather than through the link, do not forward the message on to others before verifying it, never share login credentials or card details, and block and report the number.

sections.title: Social engineering: how they knew enough to sound real
sections.text: ISEA describes social engineering as the step that usually comes before the attack: manipulating a person into giving up information without them realising a breach is happening, through impersonation by telephone, in person, or by email. It is why a fraud call can sound informed and legitimate. The routes it names are ordinary ones - conversations overheard in cafes, restaurants and offices; casual talk about yourself or about someone else; and details volunteered out of pride in an achievement or a job. Its guidance is correspondingly ordinary: avoid careless talk about personal or workplace details in public places, do not discuss other people's details with strangers, and be cautious about what a stranger asking business-sounding questions is actually collecting.

sections.title: E-wallet takeover, and the SIM swap behind it
sections.text: ISEA explains that an e-wallet permanently stores personally identifiable information - name, mobile number - along with protected details such as card numbers, a secret PIN and net-banking credentials, with only a final authorisation by OTP or biometric standing between a fraudster and a payment. Impersonation is where a fraudster uses stolen details to transact as you. The SIM swap route is the more complete takeover: the fraudster collects your information, gets your SIM blocked, walks into the operator's retail outlet with a fake identity proof, obtains a duplicate SIM, and then generates the one-time passwords themselves. Its prevention rule is a single sentence worth remembering: financial service providers and their support staff never ask a customer to share passwords or payment account numbers over an email request or a phone enquiry.

sections.title: Digital parenting: supervision that a child will still talk to you about
sections.text: ISEA frames digital parenting as supervising a child's online activity while still leaving them the independence they need, and is explicit that the balance between those two is the difficult part. Its point is that supervision only works if the child will still come to you: the goal is that they have the confidence to confide a digital problem, which means open discussion about what the apps, games and platforms are and how they are properly used, rather than rules handed down about technology the parent has not looked at. Parents are the child's first teachers and the ones the child copies, so their own habits online are part of the lesson.

sections.title: The National Commission for Women: 14490, and a complaint that is not a police case
sections.text: Not everything a woman needs is a police case, and not every woman is ready to file one. The National Commission for Women runs a 24x7 helpline on 14490 for immediate assistance and support, and accepts complaints online through its portal at ncwapps.nic.in. It takes up complaints of discrimination and atrocities against women across the range of their rights and entitlements, including matters such as domestic violence, so a woman facing online abuse that is entangled with what is happening at home has somewhere to go that handles both. This runs alongside a cybercrime complaint rather than replacing it: 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in remain the route for the cyber offence itself.
