sections.title: Free government-provided tools to clean an infected phone or computer
sections.text: After an APK was installed from a chat, a remote-access app was allowed, or a device is behaving strangely, the next step is actually cleaning it - and that does not have to be paid for. Cyber Swachhta Kendra, the Botnet Cleaning and Malware Analysis Centre run by CERT-In under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, publishes free tools at csk.gov.in. For Windows it lists free bot removal tools provided by K7 Security and by Quick Heal. For Android it lists the eScan Smartphone Safety Toolkit, and M-Kavach 2, a mobile security application developed by C-DAC Hyderabad with the support of MeitY. Download them from csk.gov.in itself rather than from a search result or a link in a message - fake security apps are one of the ways devices get infected in the first place.

sources.source_title: I4C advisories, National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit, Ministry of Home Affairs

sections.title: Digital arrest: there is no such thing in Indian law
sections.text: I4C states it plainly, and it is the one thing a frightened person needs to hear first: there is no concept of Digital Arrest under any Indian law, and real law enforcement will not arrest you digitally. The pattern it describes: a call, often from a spoofed number, from someone posing as Mumbai or Delhi Police, the CBI, the Narcotics Department, RBI, the Telecom Department or the Enforcement Directorate. They allege you are involved in something serious - contraband, drugs, fake passports or SIM cards sent through a courier company, your Aadhaar or mobile number used in illegal activity, money from a drug dealer deposited in your account, money laundering, terrorism - or that a family member has been caught. Some victims are then held in 'digital confinement', kept on a video call over Skype or WhatsApp, sometimes against a fake police-station backdrop, until they pay to make the invented case go away. I4C's precautions: never share personal or financial information on a call without verifying it, verify the caller by contacting the nearest police station yourself, and speak to a relative or friend before transferring any money. Report on 1930 or at cybercrime.gov.in.

sections.title: Calls being forwarded to a fraudster, and the code that stops it
sections.text: I4C describes a scam where criminals pose as delivery or courier agents, calling to confirm or reschedule a delivery, and then get the victim to dial a code sent by SMS beginning with *21* followed by the fraudster's mobile number. Dialling it activates call forwarding on the victim's phone, so calls from banks and the voice verification of OTPs and authentication codes for WhatsApp and Telegram go to the fraudster instead - leading to unauthorised transactions and account takeovers. The remedy is immediate and you can do it yourself: dial ##002# and all call forwarding is cancelled at once, including busy, unreachable and no-answer forwarding. Never dial a code beginning with *21*, *61* or *67* given to you by an unknown caller, do not click courier or delivery links arriving by SMS or WhatsApp, and confirm any delivery through the courier company's own website or customer-care number.

sections.title: Captcha filling and task-based 'jobs' that ask you to pay first
sections.text: I4C reports a significant rise in fraudulent captcha-filling job scams promoted on social media, job portals and messaging apps, promising high earnings for minimal effort. The sequence: you are asked to pay a registration fee, training fee or software charge to start - sometimes with a fabricated agreement to look legitimate - then given access to a fake platform with thousands of captchas to solve under strict deadlines. After some weeks the payout is refused on the grounds that your work contained inaccuracies, withdrawals are delayed or never processed, and further money is demanded for taxes, processing charges, commission or a membership upgrade, before the scammers disappear with your deposits. The red flags I4C names are: an upfront payment, unrealistic earning promises, delayed or denied withdrawals, and heavy emphasis on referring others to earn more.

sections.title: Matrimonial and dating profiles that turn into an investment pitch
sections.text: I4C's 2025 analysis of NCRP complaints found fraudsters creating fake profiles on matrimonial and dating platforms, using stolen or morphed photographs and false names, ages, professions and incomes, and presenting themselves as well-settled - working abroad, in the armed forces, or at a reputed company. They use the platform's own age and income filters to pick out people who are financially well off. Trust is built over calls, chats and video calls, sometimes with fake or edited backgrounds. Then comes the turn that distinguishes this from an ordinary romance scam: rather than asking for money directly, they create an urgent or emotional situation and steer the victim into a fraudulent investment scheme or cryptocurrency promising high returns. I4C's precautions: do a background check and a reverse image search on the photographs, share no private or financial details with anyone you have not met in person, and never transfer money for an investment on the word of someone you met online - particularly one promising unrealistic returns quickly.

sections.title: Tampered QR codes: check the address after you scan
sections.text: I4C warns that criminals tamper with both physical and digital QR codes, replacing a legitimate code with a malicious one. The victim scans what looks like the real code and is taken to a malicious site that asks for login and financial details; a malicious code may instead carry embedded malware that gives the criminal access to the device and its location along with personal and financial information. The stolen details are then used to withdraw funds or to induce fraudulent payments. The practical defence I4C gives is a habit worth forming: after scanning a QR code, look at the address that opened and check it is the site you intended and looks authentic, before entering anything.

sections.title: Banking trojans: a fake banking app that came from a real app store
sections.text: I4C describes banking trojans as malware that steals banking credentials from people using internet or mobile banking, disguised as innocent applications or web pages and built to avoid detection by staying dormant, hiding inside other files or using heavy obfuscation. The point most worth knowing: criminals mask malicious apps as legitimate ones - mobile banking and payment apps especially - and these can often be downloaded from official app stores, so 'I got it from the Play Store' is not by itself proof an app is safe. Infection also arrives through email attachments and links, drive-by downloads and deceptive pop-up windows. Once installed, the malware opens a backdoor into the device or copies credentials by spoofing the bank's login page, so what the victim types goes to the criminal's server rather than the bank.

sections.title: Overseas job offers that end in a scam compound
sections.text: The Indian Embassy in Yangon has issued repeated advisories about Indian nationals falling victim to international crime syndicates operating in the Myawaddy region on the Myanmar-Thailand border, and a newer location in the Hpa Lu area south of Myawaddy. Indians are recruited in India - and from Malaysia, the UAE and elsewhere - through job offers floated on social media and other unverified sources, then trafficked in via Thailand. The Embassy's advice is unambiguous: do not accept such job offers without consulting the Indian Embassy in the country concerned, verify the credentials of a foreign employer through that Embassy, and establish the antecedents of the recruiting agent and the company before taking up any job abroad. This is not only a financial fraud - people are held and forced to work - so a family worried about a relative who left for such a job should treat it as urgent.
